You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Purine nucleotides are ubiquitous molecules essential for all life. The de novo biosynthesis of purines is a metabolic dependency that is frequently reprogrammed in cancers and is a well-established target for chemotherapies, immune modulation and antivirals. Here, we report cryo-electron microscopy structures of the multi-domain human phosphoribosylformylglycinamidine synthase, a central purine biosynthetic enzyme and foundational feature of the purinosome metabolon. These data capture, the proposed iminophosphate intermediate and provide the structural elucidation of an ammonia channel connecting the active sites of the glutaminase and synthase domains. Analysis of this series of structures and the accompanying biochemical data also reveal the molecular features and transient conformational changes that underlie allosteric regulation and catalytic coupling of the domains. This data resolves several longstanding mechanistic questions about this enzyme class and provides a strong foundation for therapeutic development.

---

## Introduction

Purine nucleotides play essential cellular roles including the transfer of genetic information, energy storage, signaling, and as cofactors in enzyme-catalyzed reactions. They are critical to numerous physiological processes such as neurotransmission, the immune response, the regulation of cardiac function, and growth and development1–8. Purine derivatives and antimetabolites that target purine metabolism have long been used successfully as antivirals, immune modulators and chemotherapeutics9–12. The reliance on nucleotide triphosphates (NTPs) and their deoxy counterparts (dNTPs) for rapidly proliferating cells is due to the fact that these molecules are rate-limiting for numerous physiological processes, including transcription, energy storage, DNA replication and repair, ribosome biogenesis, and post-translational protein glycosylation. Increased biosynthesis of (d)NTPs is a universal, and highly druggable, feature of cancer13,14. Not surprisingly, many oncogenic drivers upregulate nucleotide biosynthesis, and these increases have been shown to promote immune evasion, metastasis, and the development of resistance to chemotherapy14–16.

Inhibitors of nucleotide biosynthetic enzymes were among the first antineoplastic agents developed and remain the core therapy for many cancer indications10,17. Despite the critical role that they play, drugs that inhibit their biosynthesis are clinically well tolerated, likely due to the presence of multiple, independent pathways to synthesize and recycle nucleotides. Numerous recent, unbiased genomic, chemical and metabolomic screening approaches have validated nucleotide metabolism as a crucial cancer vulnerability, sparked renewed interest in the field, and helped motivate many clinical trials and drug development campaigns18–26.

Purine levels are carefully regulated by coordinated control over two complementary pathways, the de novo biosynthetic pathway and the salvage pathway. The salvage pathway recycles preformed purine bases and ribose sugars to form nucleotides, while the de novo pathway builds the purine ring from small building blocks in a multi-step, energy-intensive pathway. Compared to purine salvage, the de novo biosynthetic pathway is more highly regulated and has a greater effect on cell growth27,28. Regulation of de novo biosynthesis occurs at the gene and protein level through several feed-forward and feedback mechanisms27–30. Six cytosolic enzymes catalyze the ten highly conserved steps of this pathway31,32. In addition to generating nucleotide building blocks, an increasing number of intermediates from this pathway have been implicated in important signaling cascades and non-metabolic processes33–37.

Phosphoribosylformylglycinamidine synthase (gene name PFAS, also referred to as FGAM synthase, FGAMS or PurL) catalyzes the fourth step in the de novo biosynthesis of purine nucleotides. This enzyme is directly involved in regulating purine biosynthetic rate and is known to be a core structural element of the purinosome, a biomolecular condensate that provides spatiotemporal control over purine metabolism31,32,38–41. Increased human FGAMS (HsFGAMS) expression has also been shown to promote cancer growth. In liver cancer, specifically, high expression of this protein is strongly correlated with lower survival rates13,42. In addition, FGAMS has been directly implicated in RAS-dependent cancer cell colony formation and tumor growth18,43.

Purine metabolism is regulated post-translationally by several distinct mechanisms, with HsFGAMS playing a major role in a number of these. As with other metabolic pathways, several of the nucleotide products regulate early steps in the pathway through feedback inhibition44–46. Biosynthetic flux, spatiotemporal regulation of activity, and control over reactive intermediates are also regulated, in part, by the formation and localization of the purinosome32,38–40,47. Control over purine biosynthetic enzyme kinetics, at the individual protein level, also occur through allosteric mechanisms whereby ligand binding at a location distal to the active site induces conformational changes that influence activity48–50. All but one of the enzymes of the de novo purine biosynthetic pathway are multi-domain proteins that catalyze multi-step reactions4. The activity of several of these multi-domain proteins is regulated through interdomain allostery4,44,51,52. The enzyme that catalyzes the first committed step in the pathway, phosphoribosylpyrophosphate amidotransferase, couples activity at two distinct active sites through the allosteric regulation of a channel connecting the two sites53. Such interdomain channeling functions as a means to protect labile intermediates and facilitate direct handoff of reaction products54. Parallel allosteric control of the distinct binding sites and modulation of structural features of the channel can promote efficient catalytic coupling and be a means to subtly regulate enzyme activity.

Eukaryotic FGAMS is a multi-domain protein, representative of the large PurL (lgPurl) variants of this protein, as compared to the small PurL (smPurL) proteins, which are expressed as three distinct gene products (Fig. 1a)4,55. FGAMS catalyzes the conversion of formylglycinamide ribonucleotide (FGAR) to formylglycinamidine ribonucleotide (FGAM) (Fig. 1b). In the first, amidotransferase, reaction, ammonia is liberated from glutamine and directed to the synthase domain, where it is added to FGAR in an ATP-dependent reaction56. The transfer of ammonia between the two active sites is facilitated by a putative ammonia channel56. The presence of the channel is supported by computational and kinetic analyses, although it has not yet been physically observed nor is it clear how channel entry and exit are regulated57. FGAMS also harbors an N-terminal domain with an, as yet, unestablished role.

In this work, we describe three Cryo-EM structures of HsFGAMS, from 3.2 to 3.3 Å resolution, that capture distinct functional states and important pathway intermediates. These structures of FGAMS reveal the location and architecture of the ammonia channel and capture the proposed iminophosphate intermediate. These data also implicate the N-terminal domain as a key element involved in allosteric control of FGAMS activity. The structures and supporting kinetic analyses reveal a putative mechanism that couples the chemistry of the active sites through substrate-induced conformational changes, controlling formation of the ammonia channel as well as substrate entry and exit.

---

## Results

Expression and initial characterization of HsFGAMS
Full details about the cloning, expression, and purification of HsFGAMS are included in the supplementary information. Briefly, HsFGAMS was expressed as a C-terminally FLAG-tagged protein from HEK 293T cells and purified using immobilized affinity chromatography (Fig. 1c). Unlike the homologs from E. coli and S. typhimurium, which show a high level of basal glutaminase activity55,58–60, HsFGAMS does not exhibit observable glutaminase activity in the absence of the co-substrate FGAR (Fig. 1d). With FGAR present, the enzyme turns over glutamine with a KM of 189 ± 20 μM and kcat of 1.0 ± 0.04 s−1. Although the synthase activity of FGAMS is difficult to measure directly, we recently developed a mechanism-based assay that measures dephosphorylation of 6,8-difluoro-4-methylumbelliferyl phosphate as a surrogate for synthase activity42. Using this assay, we determined that an anomeric mixture of the substrate, α/β-FGAR, competitively binds to HsFGAMS with an IC50 of 148 ± 4 μM. As FGAMS is known to be selective for the β-FGAR anomer59, the KM for this substrate is expected to be approximately half this value.

Cryo-EM structure of the HsFGAMS-AMPPNP binary complex
To elucidate the molecular features underlying FGAMS function and as a basis for future drug discovery efforts, we sought to solve structures of FGAMS in functionally relevant states. Prior studies of S. typhimurium FGAMS (StPurL) include unliganded (3UGJ), glutamine-bound (1T3T), and glutamine/AMP-PNP (non-hydrolyzable ATP analogue) bound (3UMM) X-ray crystal structures60. Using Cryo-EM, we solved the structures of (1) HsFGAMS with AMP-PNP bound (referred to as the binary complex); (2) HsFGAMS in complex with the iminophosphate reaction intermediate and adenosine diphosphate (ADP) (referred to as the ternary complex); and 3) HsFGAMS with glutamyl thioester, AMP-PNP and FGAR bound (referred to as the quaternary complex) (Fig. 2). The ligand combinations were chosen to map the distinct steps of the catalytic mechanism, stabilize transition/intermediate states and to identify the long-range allosteric regulation network essential for the enzyme to reach its catalytically active state.

The binary complex was prepared by incubating HsFGAMS with 5 mM AMP-PNP on ice for 4 hours prior to grid preparation. We obtained an initial 3.35 Å map using C1 symmetry (Supplementary Figs. 1–3), with further 3D classification followed by non-uniform refinement yielding an improved 3.31 Å map. The final model was built using the predicted HsFGAMS structure from AlphaFold61 as a starting model. Full data collection parameters and refinement statistics are provided in Supplementary Table 1. Analysis of the binary complex structure confirms that HsFGAMS is a single polypeptide organized into three domains (Fig. 2a, b), similar to the homologous prokaryotic lgPurL structures (Supplementary Fig. 4)56. In addition to the glutaminase domain (GD, residues 1005–1335, Fig. 2 and Supplementary Fig. 5a) and synthase domain (SD, residues 173–1004, Fig. 2 and Supplementary Fig. 5b), is an N-terminal domain (NTD, Fig. 2 and Supplementary Fig. 5c) comprising residues 1–164. The SD has the expected pseudo 2-fold symmetry characteristic of this domain, consistent with a gene duplication event during the evolutionary history of this protein56. The synthase active site is found in one half of the SD, situated in a cleft formed by three subdomains (Supplementary Figs. 5b). In the other half of the SD, occupying a symmetry-related nucleotide-binding site, is an auxiliary ADP molecule (Supplementary Fig. 5b). The map shows clear density for the ADP and three associated Mg2+ ions (Fig. 3a and Supplementary Fig. 3). As there is no evidence linking this nucleotide to an enzymatic or regulatory function, the ADP is believed to play only a structural role or be a vestigial remnant of the putative duplication event that led to the formation of the SD62. The clear density distinguishing this molecule as an ADP in the binary complex, the enclosed nature of the binding site, and the fact that ADP was not present in any solutions used during purification or structural work, suggests that this molecule is incorporated during protein folding and cannot be competitively displaced by similar nucleotides, such as AMP-PNP (Fig. 3a and Supplementary Fig. 5b). The identity of the bound nucleotide was confirmed as ADP in HsFGAMS by analysis of denatured apoprotein by HPLC (Supplementary Fig. 5b).

In the binary complex of HsFGAMS, the ATP-binding site is occupied by AMP-PNP (Fig. 3b and Supplementary Fig. 3). The nucleotide binding pocket, which sits at the interface of two subdomains (Supplementary Fig. 5b), is composed of a hydrophobic pocket surrounding the adenine base (Fig. 3b, F235, F251, and F269) abutted by a loop (267–274) that forms hydrogen bonds with ribose hydroxyls and phosphate oxygen atoms. A comparison to the AMP-PCP bound PurL structure from T. maritima (TmPurL, PDB code 2HS4) suggests that additional interactions with, and charge stabilization of, the phosphates may be contributed by a metal cation that is not observable in our maps (Supplementary Fig. 6a). While the overall architecture of both the auxiliary ADP binding site and ATP binding site in the HsFGAMS SD is relatively well conserved with those of S. typhimurium and T. maritima PurL, there are several subtle but clear differences (Supplementary Fig. 6a, b). In the ATP binding site, interactions mediated by residues on the loop spanning 267-274 are distinct and dissimilar to those observed in the prokaryotic homologs (Supplementary Fig. 6a). In addition, a partially resolved, unstructured catalytic loop (C-loop, 461–479) is observed near the synthase site in the binary complex (Fig. 2a). For the prokaryote structure, this region was observed to become ordered only in the presence of FGAR at the synthase site55. Computational studies performed with the full length StPurL proposed that this loop plays a role in signal transmission and catalytic coupling between the distant active sites57.

The GD of HsFGAMS (Fig. 2b and Supplementary Fig. 5a) contains the conserved catalytic triad characteristic of the class I amidotransferase superfamily63. The catalytic cysteine (C1158) resides on a structural motif known as a “nucleophilic elbow”63. The GD interacts with the NTD primarily through hydrophobic contacts (W62, N103, I104, V107, and T111 of the NTD and V1122, G1128, A1131, and F1135 of the GD) while a series of hydrogen bonds span the GD-SD interface (N95, P99, and N102 of the NTD and D488, E490, G545, and D546 of the SD). Close examination of the HsFGAMS binary complex reveals a loop region (designated loop L1) from the NTD blocking the glutaminase active site (Supplementary Fig. 6c). The location of the L1 loop in the absence of substrate appears to be driven by an interaction between H14 on L1 and Y1237 of the GD. The presence of this 11-residue loop, and an additional, longer, solvent exposed loop (designated loop L4), are major differences setting HsFGAMS apart from the prokaryotic homologs, which do not possess these features (Supplementary Fig. 6d). However, despite low sequence identity and the presence of the loop inserts, the NTD of HsFGAMS has an overall fold that is structurally homologous to the prokaryotic PurLs of known structure (Supplementary Fig. 6e). The position of loop L1 in HsFGAMS, and its absence in prokaryotes, is suggestive of a putative role in regulating access to the glutaminase site that is distinct to the human enzyme.

Cryo-EM structure of the HsFGAMS ternary complex with trapped iminophosphate intermediate
Production of the FGAM product by FGAMS requires two separate reactions at distinct active sites (Fig. 1b). Ammonia liberated in the GD is added to FGAR in an ATP-dependent reaction. The mechanism of the synthase reaction is proposed to proceed via an activated iminophosphate intermediate55. To evaluate the architecture and allosteric regulation of the HsFGAMS SD, we prepared samples and collected Cryo-EM data for the protein with FGAR and ATP, but lacking the co-substrate glutamine. Details about sample preparation and processing are provided in the supplementary information and methods. After processing we obtained a 3.22 Å map (Fig. 2c and Supplementary Figs. 2b, 7 and 8), that was further post-processed using DeepEMhancer with individual half maps as input64, revealing additional features (Supplementary Fig. 9). The resulting map showed clearly resolved coulombic potential for a trapped iminophosphate intermediate together with an ADP molecule (Figs. 2c, d, and 3c), and a well ordered C-loop (Fig. 3d and Supplementary Fig. 8). Other alternative ligand binding modes, including ATP and FGAR or FGAR, ADP and phosphate, were not consistent with the observed density (Supplementary Figs. 10a, b). A comparison of the HsFGAMS ternary complex synthase site to that of TmPurL in complex with FGAR and AMP-PCP (PDB code 2HS4) reveals a similar binding position and orientation of the ligands and C-loop (Supplementary Fig. 10c). The ordered C-loop adopts a closed conformation in this ternary complex, shielding the synthase site and the reactive iminophosphate intermediate (Fig. 3e). This intermediate and the ADP molecule were observed to be present perpendicular to each other in the synthase site (Fig. 3e). The density also revealed the likely presence of an alternate conformer of ADP in the active pocket (Fig. 3c, e). Q485 on the C-loop makes key H-bonding interactions with the H311 and the formylglycinamide of the trapped intermediate (Fig. 3e). This interaction forms a putative anchor point that could drive the C-loop into a closed conformation. Prior computational studies using StPurL also implicated these two residues in a putative gating mechanism that controls transient channel formation65.

The SD of FGAMS belongs to the PurM superfamily of proteins, which includes selenophosphate synthase (SelD), iron-nickel hydrogenase maturation protein (HypE), and thiamine phosphate kinase (ThiL), among others66. These proteins are related by their signature DX4GAXPATP binding motif and the putative formation of an iminophosphate intermediate during catalysis. The trapped iminophosphate in the structure of the HsFGAMS ternary complex provides structural confirmation of this reaction intermediate. For FGAMS specifically, two alternate enzyme mechanisms have been proposed (Supplementary Fig. 11)67. These involve either a tetrahedral intermediate (Supplementary Fig. 11; path a) or the iminophosphate intermediate (Supplementary Fig. 11; path b) as observed in the HsFGAMS ternary complex structure. Our data, collected in the absence of an ammonia source, are consistent with phosphorylation of the δ-carbonyl of FGAR to form an iminophosphate intermediate.

Cryo-EM structure of the HsFGAMS quaternary complex with Glutamine, AMP-PNP, and FGAR
To further evaluate substrate binding, mechanism, and cooperative regulation of the distinct active sites, we incubated the protein with L-glutamine, AMP-PNP, and α/β-FGAR prior to grid preparation and data collection. From a total of 184,653 particles, we obtained a map at 3.19 Å using C1 symmetry (Fig. 2e and Supplementary Figs. 2c, 12 and 13). Further post-processing was performed using DeepEMHancer64, leading to improvements in the map, particularly in a hydrophobic linker, 3-helix bundle near the synthase site and the partially disordered C-loop (Figs. 2f, 4a and Supplementary Fig. 14). In the glutaminase active site the map was similarly well resolved to enable modeling of the substrate, which was trapped as a glutamyl thioester intermediate (Fig. 4b and Supplementary Fig. 13). In the synthase active site, there was clearly discernible coulomb potential to build the AMP-PNP and FGAR ligands (Fig. 4c, and Supplementary Fig. 13), as well as the majority of the C-loop structure (Fig. 4a–c). Similar to what was observed for the ternary complex, the AMP-PNP ligand could be built into two alternate conformations (Supplementary Fig. 13). The FGAR molecule sits perpendicular to the nucleotide, and is held in place primarily through H-bonding interactions from both the synthase binding site residues and the C-loop (Fig. 4c). When compared to the structure of the T. maritima PurL (PDB code 2HS4), the C-loop of HsFGAMS is in a more open conformation (Fig. 4d), potentially due to substrate binding at the distant GD. This configuration of the C-loop repositions Q485 away from H311 (Fig. 4c), disrupting the H-bond interaction between these two residues. This is consistent with a putative role for Q485 in regulation of intraprotein signal transmission, as proposed in previous studies65. The glutamyl thioester intermediate observed in the glutaminase active site is engaged in the primarily hydrophobic binding pocket that is highly conserved across species (Fig. 4d). Clear density was also observed at H-bonding distance from the OE2 atom of the thioester, modeled here as a water molecule (Fig. 4b, W). This marks the putative location of the initial site of the ammonia molecule immediately after liberation from glutamine.

Formation of the iminophosphate intermediate signals the GD via structural rearrangements in the NTD
The function of the NTD in FGAMS has long been unresolved. Comparison of the structures of the different states of HsFGAMS reveals distinct differences, particular between the binary (AMP-PNP bound) and ternary (iminophosphate and ADP) complexes (Fig. 5). Upon binding of the synthase substrates and formation of the iminophosphate intermediate, the NTD shifts substantially, rotating approximately 10° with respect to the GD (Fig. 5a). Accompanying this domain motion is a similar shift in a 3-helix bundle of the SD that abuts the C-loop (Fig. 5a). Conversely, other than a slight disordering of the C-loop, the overall structure of HsFGAMS in the quaternary complex was very similar to that of the binary complex (Fig. 5b).

Further analysis of these structural differences reveals several functionally relevant implications. In the ternary complex, one edge of the 3-helix bundle moves into proximity with the C-loop, forming new H-bonding interactions, specifically between G462, A465, and S468 of the C-loop and Q224 and E228 of the 3-helix bundle (Supplementary Fig. 15). The ordering and repositioning of the C-loop in the ternary complex result in a well-structured pocket surrounding the iminophosphate (Fig. 3e), presumably to protect the reactive intermediate. In addition, residues of the C-loop, which spans the region between the NTD and the 3-helix bundle, form a cation-π stacking interaction with conserved residues of the NTD (Supplementary Fig. 16). Based on the structures and supported by previous analysis of mutants57, this network plays a crucial role in intraprotein signaling between the NTD and C-loop.

This newly created NTD:C-loop interface is accompanied by conformational changes in the putative oxyanion loop, a recurring and short-lived feature common to nearly all glutaminases that stabilizes the oxyanion transition state (Fig. 6a and Supplementary Figs. 17a–d)68. Upon formation of the ternary complex, the interactions between the oxyanion loop and nearby Ω-loop, which harbors the signaling residue N107457,65, are disrupted. This results in an approximately 90° flip of the oxyanion loop and creation of the putative oxyanion hole (Fig. 6b–d). Based on the expected position of the oxyanion, movement of a section of the oxyanion loop would be necessary to accommodate the tetrahedral transition state. Our structures indicate that stabilizing interactions would be contributed through hydrogen bonding interactions with the amide nitrogen atoms of N1159 and one of the loop residues. Formation of the oxyanion hole in this manner is a proposed mechanism for substrate-dependent allosteric regulation in other glutamine amidotransferases and related enzymes, such as imidazole glycerol phosphate synthase69,70. The HsFGAMS structures suggest a critical role for the G1115-N1074 interaction in stabilizing the closed conformation of the oxyanion loop (Fig. 6b). This is consistent with previous mutational studies performed with the analogous residues in StPurL65. Upon glutamyl thioester intermediate formation, as observed in the quaternary structure of HsFGAMS, the oxyanion loop reverts back to the resting state, orienting residues G1115, G1116, and F1117 to help position and stabilize the intermediate (Fig. 6e, f).

In addition to the allosteric control through transient oxyanion stabilization, we also observed that entry to the glutaminase active site is regulated by two gates. Gate 1 is composed of H14 on the L1 loop of the NTD and Y1237 of the GD, while Y1202 and F1117 of the GD comprise gate 2 (Fig. 6a). The changes in the NTD of the ternary complex result in disorder in loop L1 (Fig. 6c), providing the needed flexibility for gating motions of H14. Similarly, these changes also impact the positioning of Y1237, yielding an open state of one of the gates (Fig. 6c, gate 1). At the same time, the loop flipping that controls transient oxyanion hole formation moves F1117 and Y1202. The latter, in particular, swings approximately 90° away from Y1202, opening this second gate (Fig. 6c, gate 2). Both of these gates return to the closed state in the quaternary complex of HsFGAMS (Fig. 6e). Note that the mechanism for gating through gate 1 is distinct to mammals, as the loop L1 region is not conserved in lower organisms (Supplementary Fig. 6c, d).

Catalytic coupling through transient ammonia channel formation
The chemistry at the synthase site of FGAMS requires delivery of the ammonia molecule produced at the distinct and distant glutaminase site. Delivery of the ammonia has been proposed to travel between the two active sites through a putative ammonia channel in the enzyme (Fig. 1b). To date, however, this channel has not been experimentally observed. In the HsFGAMS quaternary complex structure, we elucidate the architecture of this hydrophobic transient channel that passes near the auxiliary ADP binding site (Fig. 7a and Supplementary Fig. 18) using CAVER 3.0.2 PyMOL plugin71. The channel location and composition are consistent with what was predicted by MD simulations for the StPurL system (Supplementary Fig. 18)57.

Comparison of the quaternary structure to the binary and ternary complex structures reveal several key structural changes driving transient channel formation. Structure analysis showed that after glutamyl thioester intermediate formation in GD, the oxyanion loop flipped back to regain its original conformation and helped to stabilize the carbonyl group of the glutamyl moiety via hydrogen bonding interaction through its G1116 residue (Fig. 6e, f) and by closing gate 1 and gate 2 to protect the thioester intermediate in the GD (Fig. 6e). This oxyanion loop resting conformation further reverted the signal to the NTD by rotating it back by ~10o to go back in its previous conformation (Fig. 5b) via disrupting the GD and NTD interface (Fig. 6a and Supplementary Figs. 17a–d). This NTD/GD interface disruption forced the C-loop to move back in its unstructured conformation, similar to the HsPFAS-AMPPNP binary state. From moving fully ordered to fully disordered state, there is a stage when the C-loop is partially disordered. At this stage, two other gates; gate 3 (R1300-D685) at the top of the channel (Fig. 7b) and gate 4 (Q485-H311) at the bottom of the channel (Fig. 7c), are opened, which were observed to be closed in other two HsPFAS binary and ternary complexes solved here and in the previously solved StPurL and smPurL crystal structures also55,56. In brief, a salt bridge between R1300 and D685 reorganizes to form the opening of the channel at the glutaminase active site (Fig. 7b). At the synthase end of the channel, H311 is observed to block the exit in both the binary and ternary complexes, but subtle changes to Q485 disrupt the H311-Q485 interaction, opening the gate at the synthase end of the channel (Fig. 7c). The opening and closing events of these conserved gates were also highlighted in previous MD simulation studies57,65. Moreover, the mutational studies performed on gate 3 in StPurL showed a high ammonia channeling efficiency, highlighting the role of this gate in controlling ammonia release into the channel, while the mutants of gate 4 showed its dual role in gating and signal transduction to the glutaminase site65. In addition to these dual gates, additional motions were observed in the secondary structure elements on which the conserved channel lining residues reside. These residues include N394, P399, V400, S390, E398, D333, A348, T327, Y350, P423, T325, R330, T310 and M425. Additional bottleneck residues M425, Y350, and E398 obstruct the channel in the binary and ternary complexes, but change positions subtly in the quaternary complex structure to provide a clear path for the ammonia to traverse (Fig. 7a, d, and e). Mutational and crystallographic studies were previously performed on the conserved channel lining residue (V400 in HsFGAMS and V333 in StPurL) that showed a remarkable effect on the channel efficiency72. In this case, a valine to isoleucine mutation constricted the channel by ~2 Å, leading to a decrease in the synthase activity by ~20%72. Collectively, the structural changes precipitated by substrate binding and formation of the quaternary complex lead to the transient formation of the ammonia channel and provide additional gating mechanisms to regulate FGAMS activity. This type of enzyme control is not without precedent. Similar substrate-driven domain motions lead to the formation of an ammonia channel in the bacterial glucosamine-6-phosphate synthase73,74.

To confirm the role of the gating residues and transient channel formation, we generated a series of HsFGAMS mutants and characterized their relative kinetics. For all of the mutants, we determined the basal glutaminase activity, the ATP and FGAR dependent glutamate production, and overall FGAM synthesis rate (Supplementary Fig. 19a–c, respectively). While the basal rate of glutaminase activity of HsFGAMS is very low, removal of a short section of loop L1 containing gate 1 residue H14 (Δ12–15) or mutation of either of the gate 2 residues (Y1202F, F1117A), leads to a substantial increase in background glutaminase activity (Supplementary Fig. 19a). Leakage of ammonia through gate 2 is at a much higher rate, consistent with an overall motive force favoring ammonia flow from the GD to the synthase active site. As expected, the presence of ATP and FGAR does not have a large impact on the glutaminase rate for these mutants (Supplementary Fig. 19b). These mutants, however, do substantially decrease the overall rate of FGAM synthesis (Supplementary Fig. 19c). This disruption in the gating and coupling efficiency of the two domains through these subtle changes (Supplementary Fig. 19d) illustrates the importance of the tight control over substrate access and transit in FGAMS (Supplementary Figs. 19e, f). As a comparison, mutation of one of the bottleneck residues (M425K), which sits in the interior of the channel, has little impact on the glutaminase or synthase activity (Supplementary Figs. 19a–c).

## Methods

General methods
Unless otherwise stated, all chemicals and reagents were from Fisher bioreagents, Merck-Millipore, Sigma-Aldrich, Fluka, and Acros Organics. All restriction enzymes were purchased from New England Biolabs or Thermo Scientific. The C-term DDK(Flag)-tagged human FGAMS (HsFGAMS) (accession #NM_012393.3) plasmid in pCMV6-entry vector was purchased from OriGene. HEK-293 cells (CRL-3216) used for protein expression were purchased from ATCC®.

Expression and FLAG affinity purification of human FGAMS
The C-terminally flag-tagged HsFGAMS protein was expressed in HEK-293 cells and purified using Flag-affinity purification as reported previously42. In brief, five 182 cm2 polystyrene tissue culture flasks having 0.22 μm vented filter cap (Genesee Scientific) were each seeded with 1 × 106 HEK-293 cells in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle’s Medium (DMEM) supplemented with 10% Fetal Bovine Serum (FBS) and 1% penicillin streptomycin (PS). Cells were grown at 37 °C in 5% CO2. The next day, when the cell confluence was ~80%, the media was replaced, and each flask was transfected with a complex of HsFGAMS plasmid and PEI transfection reagent (in a ratio of 1:3 in serum free media). The media was again replaced 24 h’ post-transfection and incubated at 37 °C in 5% CO2. Cells were harvested after 72 h and stored at −80 °C until purification. The protein was purified using 1X PBS (phosphate buffered saline), pH 7.4, running buffer. Cells were re-suspended in running buffer having 1X protease inhibitor cocktail (Roche) and sonicated twice for 25 s each with a 1-min pause and 40% amplitude. The cell lysate was centrifuged at 19840 rcf for 30 min and the supernatant was incubated with pre-equilibrated Flag affinity resin at 4 °C. After 2 h, the protein bound resin was collected by centrifugation at 770 rcf for 15 min and the supernatant was transferred into another vial. The Flag resin was washed 4 times with 1X PBS to remove loosely bound impurities. The protein was eluted by incubating the resin with 1 mL elution buffer (100 μg/mL Flag peptide in running buffer) at 4 °C for 30 min. The purity of the eluted protein was determined using 10% SDS-PAGE. Fractions deemed to be greater than 95% purity were pooled, concentrated using a 50k MWCO centrifugal concentrator (Millipore), and the concentration was measured using a nanodrop spectrophotometer at 280 nm.

Size exclusion chromatography (SEC)
SEC was performed at 25 °C using an Agilent 1100 series HPLC instrument with an analytical Zenix SEC-300 column (4.6 × 300 mm, Sepax). The column was pre-equilibrated and eluted in filtered and degassed SEC buffer (1X PBS; pH 7.4). HsFGAMS protein (0.6 mg/mL) in 20 μL of buffer was injected and eluted with a flow rate of 0.350 mL/min. A standard curve, generated using Thyroglobulin (669 kDa), Ferritin (443 kDa), Aldolase (158 kDa), Conalbumin (75 kDa), and RNase A (13.7 kDa), was generated and used to determine the approximate values for molecular weight.

Preparation of HsFGAMS complexes
The binary complex of HsFGAMS with AMPPNP was generated by incubating purified protein (0.7 mg/mL final concentration) with 10 mM AMPPNP. The ternary complex was generated by incubating purified HsFGAMS (0.7 mg/mL final concentration) with 10 mM ATP and 2 mM α/β-FGAR (1:1 anomeric mixture). The quaternary complex was prepared by incubating 0.5 mg/mL HsFGAMS with 10 mM L-Glutamine, 10 mM AMPPNP, and 2 mM α/β-FGAR. The reactions were setup in 1X PBS pH 7.4 buffer at 4 °C for 4 h followed by a short spin at 770 rcf, followed by further incubation on ice for 30 min.

Grid preparation and Cryo-EM data collection
4–5 μL of each complex was applied to a glow discharged Quantifoil R 1.2/1.3, UT, 300 mesh gold grid (Electron Microscopy Sciences) at a concentration of 0.5 to 0.7 mg/mL on a Vitrobot Mark IV system (Thermo Fisher Scientific) set at 4 °C, 100% humidity, blot time of 5 s and blot force of 0. The grids were screened for ice quality, as well as particle distribution and density, before setting up data collection. Images were collected on a 300 kV Titan Krios G2 microscope equipped with K3 Summit detector (Gatan) in super-resolution mode with binning 2 and CDS, along with a Gatan BioContinuum GIF energy filter (slit width of 20 eV) at The Hormel Institute with an exposure of 1.7–2 s. Image stacks comprising 40 frames were recorded at an estimated total dose of 50 e-/Å2. Automated data collection was carried out using the EPU 3.2.0.4776REL software (Thermo Fisher Scientific) at a nominal magnification of 130000X corresponding to a calibrated pixel size of 0.652 Å with a defocus range from -0.75 to -2.5 μm.

Data processing, class reconstruction, and model building of HsFGAMS complexes
Dose-fractionated movies were gain normalized, drift corrected, summed, and dose weighted using Patch motion correction module in CryoSPARC75. The contrast transfer function (CTF) was estimated for each summed image using the Patch CTF module. For HsFGAMS/AMPPNP binary complex, particles were picked and extracted from the dose-weighted images with box size of 320 px using CryoSPARC blob picker and particle extraction. The particles were curated using two rounds of CryoSPARC 2D classification (number of classes, N=50), resulting in 3,595,274 particles. The templates selected using Select 2D module were further used for particle picking using template picker module and extracted using the same box size resulting in 7,325,050 particles. High quality particles were selected using 4 cycles of 2D classification and selection. Initial models were generated using CryoSPARC ab initio reconstruction on full set of good 1,010,335 particles using C1 symmetry (N=3). The largest class of curated particles were used for homogenous refinement. This was further refined using non-uniform refinement that resulted in a map of 3.35 Å76. This map was used as a template for 3D classification (N=4) out of which particles from classes 1–3 were pooled and refined using non-uniform refinement with C1 symmetry, resulting in a 3.31 Å map. Further local map sharpening and denoising were performed using deepEMhancer tool in CryoSPARC. The alpha-fold predicted structure of HsFGAMS was used as a primary model and docked in the final map using ChimeraX77. For the HsFGAMS/Iminophosphate/ADP ternary complex, particles were picked and extracted from the dose-weighted images with box size of 320 px using the HsFGAMS/AMPPNP binary complex 2D templates. The particles were curated using 4 rounds of CryoSPARC 2D classification (number of classes, N=50). Initial models were generated using CryoSPARC ab initio reconstruction on a full set of 1,137,400 particles using C1 symmetry (N=5). The largest class of curated particles was used for non-uniform refinement that resulted in a map of 3.22 Å. This map was used as a template for 3D classification (N=4), out of which, the largest class was refined using non-uniform refinement with C1 symmetry, resulting in a 3.22 Å map. The HsFGAMS/AMPPNP binary complex structure solved above was used as a primary model and docked in the final map using ChimeraX. For the HsFGAMS/L-Glutamine/AMPPNP/FGAR quaternary complex, particles were picked and extracted from the dose-weighted images with box size of 320 px using the HsFGAMS/AMPPNP binary complex 2D templates and particle extraction. The particles were curated using 2 rounds of CryoSPARC 2D classification (number of classes, N=50). Initial models were generated using CryoSPARC ab initio reconstruction on the full set of 1,366,039 particles using C1 symmetry (N=4). The largest curated class was used for homogeneous refinement and followed by non-uniform refinement that resulted in a map of 3.21 Å. This map was used as a template for 3D classification (N=10), out of which three classes were pooled and refined using homogeneous followed by non-uniform refinement with C1 symmetry, resulting in a 3.19 Å map. In this case also, the HsFGAMS/AMPPNP binary complex structure solved above was used as a primary model and docked in the final map using ChimeraX. The manual model building for all three complexes was done in WinCoot78, and the models were refined in Phenix79. The refined models were validated with MolProbity80 within Phenix. Figures were prepared using UCSF Chimera, ChimeraX, and Pymol 2.4 (The PyMOL Molecular Graphics System, Version 1.2r3pre, Schrödinger, LLC).

Mutagenesis
All mutants were designed either by Gibson’s method81 or by traditional cloning. Native plasmids served as a template, and gene fragments were amplified using Phusion or Q5 high fidelity DNA polymerase. For the Δ12_15 and M425K mutants, the amplified fragments were assembled using 2X HiFi DNA assembly master mix (New England Biolab) for 1 h at 50 °C. For the F1117A and Δ12_15/Y1202F mutants, the amplified gene was digested with Mfe-I and Mlu-I restriction enzymes and ligated into the pCMV6-ENTRY vector using T4 DNA ligase. DH5α cells were directly transformed using the assembled and ligated genes to obtain the mutant plasmid. The inserted mutations were confirmed by Sanger sequencing.

Assay for glutamate production
The glutamate production of HsFGAMS was coupled with a standard glutamate dehydrogenase assay, where glutamate produced from HsFGAMS is converted to α-ketoglutarate in the presence of NAD+. Here, we used 3-acetylpyridiene adenine dinucleotide (APAD) in place of NAD+ because APAD has a more significant oxidation potential than NAD+, is more effectively reduced, and is more stable than NAD+. A 50 μL reaction was setup containing 20 mM Tris pH 7.5, 20 mM MgCl2, 80 mM KCl, 10 mM ATP, 1 mM α/β-FGAR, 1 mM APAD, 2 U L-Glutamate dehydrogenase, 1 mM L-Glutamine, and 1 μM test enzyme according to the previously reported protocol59. The glutamate production was determined using a coupled glutamate dehydrogenase assay82 by monitoring the reduction of APAD at 363 nm in Spectramax M2 plate reader for 30 min. To determine the kinetic parameters, the concentration of L-Glutamine was varied from 30 μM to 1 mM. The concentration of glutamate produced was determined by Beer Lambert’s equation (A=εCl where A is absorbance, ε is molar extinction coefficient of product, C is concentration of the product and l is path length in mm) using a molar extinction coefficient of 9100 M−1 cm−1.

Assay for FGAM synthesis
FGAM production was determined using a previously established protocol59. In brief, the conversion of FGAR to FGAM by HsFGAMS was coupled with TrifGART enzyme that further converts FGAM to aminoimidazole ribonucleotide (AIR). A reaction mixture of 100 μL having 20 mM HEPES buffer pH 7.5, 20 mM MgCl2, 80 mM KCl, 10 mM ATP, 1 μM α/β-FGAR, 5 mM L-Glutamine, 0.5 μM test enzyme, and 1 μM TrifGART enzyme was incubated at 37 °C for 30 min. The reaction was quenched by adding 15 μL of 20% trichloroacetic acid (pH 1.4). Precipitates were removed by centrifugation, and AIR formation was determined by coupling using a standard Bratton–Marshall’s assay83. The intensity of pink color, measured at 500 nm on a Spectramax M2 plate reader, was used to quantify product formation.

Transient ammonia channel identification
The transient ammonia channel has been identified using CAVER 3.0.2 PyMOL plugin using default parameters, i.e., probe radius of 0.9 Å, shell depth 4 Å, shell radius of 3 Å, and clustering threshold of 3.5. The channel connecting the two distant active sites in GD and FD was identified only in HsFGAMS quaternary complex cryo-EM structure reported here.

HPLC analysis of nucleotide binding in apo FGAMS
To determine the identity of the bound nucleotide in the apo FGAMS protein an aliquot of HsFGAMS protein purified as described above (in the absence of any nucleotides) was boiled for 20 min and centrifuged to remove precipitates. This sample was evaluated with ion exchange HPLC (Agilent 1100 system) with a 4.6 × 250 mm BioSAX NP5 column (Agilent) running a gradient from 25 to 300 mM NaCl in 20 mM Tris, pH 8, over 20 min at 1 mL/min. The elution time of the sample was compared to authentic standards of ATP, ADP, and AMP-PNP.

### Reviewer 3

The manuscript describes structures of the human de novo purine biosynthetic enzyme phosphoribosylglycinamidine synthase (hFGAMS) from cryo-EM analysis.
The 3-domain monomeric enzyme (>1300 residues) catalyzes a multi-step reaction: ATP-dependent formation of an imino-phosphate intermediate of the FGAR substrate in a synthase active site, release of ammonia by glutamine hydrolysis in a glutaminase active site, diffusion of ammonia through a channel in the enzyme, and attack of ammonia on the imino-phosphate to release the FGAM product. The synthase and glutaminase active sites are >20 Å apart. A long-standing question has been the coordination of the catalytic steps, as no glutamine hydrolysis occurs in absence of the FGAR substrate.
The authors have considerable experience with FGAMS, and here they cryo-trapped 3 substrate complexes on EM grids by judicious choices of reaction conditions. The EM maps are of high quality (resolution 3.1 – 3.3 Å by 0.143 FSC). They include
binary complex of AMP-PNP in the synthase acive site,
ternary complex with the imino-phosphate intermediate & ADP in the synthase active site,
quaternary complex with AMP-PNP & FGAR in the synthase active site and the acyl-enzyme intermediate (Cys-Glu thioester) in the glutaminase active site.
Most of the Results section is devoted to a detailed analysis of small structural features of the 3 complexes. Nearly all the structure regions described have good density in the EM maps.
FGAMS is well conserved from bacteria to humans, so some of the substrate poses can be validated in published higher-resolution crystal structures of prokaryotic homologs. This aspect of the interpretation seems very solid. The changes in structure with addition of substrates are very small. Visualizing the human enzyme in several catalytic states is a substantial advance in our understanding of catalytic coupling in hFGAMS, but – in my view – less of an advance than the authors claim.
The structural details were challenging to understand, even after superposition of the 3 models, because several elements of structure are not defined (loop 1, loop 4, C-loop, catalytic triad, oxyanion loop, Ω-loop, 3-helix bundle, gate 1, gate 2, gate 3, gate 4). This makes it very challenging to look at the structures and evaluate the authors’ model for catalytic coupling and ammonia travel.

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications.

You previously reviewed this paper and raised several concerns. The authors have now submitted a revised manuscript along with a detailed point-by-point response. Your task is to write your updated review after carefully reading:
  1. The revised paper
  2. Your original Round 1 review
  3. The authors' point-by-point response

In your updated review, explicitly state which concerns have been adequately addressed and which remain outstanding. Be specific.

## Paper

## Abstract

Purine nucleotides are ubiquitous molecules essential for all life. The de novo biosynthesis of purines is a metabolic dependency that is frequently reprogrammed in cancers and is a well-established target for chemotherapies, immune modulation and antivirals. Here, we report cryo-electron microscopy structures of the multi-domain human phosphoribosylformylglycinamidine synthase, a central purine biosynthetic enzyme and foundational feature of the purinosome metabolon. These data capture, the proposed iminophosphate intermediate and provide the structural elucidation of an ammonia channel connecting the active sites of the glutaminase and synthase domains. Analysis of this series of structures and the accompanying biochemical data also reveal the molecular features and transient conformational changes that underlie allosteric regulation and catalytic coupling of the domains. This data resolves several longstanding mechanistic questions about this enzyme class and provides a strong foundation for therapeutic development.

---

## Introduction

Purine nucleotides play essential cellular roles including the transfer of genetic information, energy storage, signaling, and as cofactors in enzyme-catalyzed reactions. They are critical to numerous physiological processes such as neurotransmission, the immune response, the regulation of cardiac function, and growth and development1–8. Purine derivatives and antimetabolites that target purine metabolism have long been used successfully as antivirals, immune modulators and chemotherapeutics9–12. The reliance on nucleotide triphosphates (NTPs) and their deoxy counterparts (dNTPs) for rapidly proliferating cells is due to the fact that these molecules are rate-limiting for numerous physiological processes, including transcription, energy storage, DNA replication and repair, ribosome biogenesis, and post-translational protein glycosylation. Increased biosynthesis of (d)NTPs is a universal, and highly druggable, feature of cancer13,14. Not surprisingly, many oncogenic drivers upregulate nucleotide biosynthesis, and these increases have been shown to promote immune evasion, metastasis, and the development of resistance to chemotherapy14–16.

Inhibitors of nucleotide biosynthetic enzymes were among the first antineoplastic agents developed and remain the core therapy for many cancer indications10,17. Despite the critical role that they play, drugs that inhibit their biosynthesis are clinically well tolerated, likely due to the presence of multiple, independent pathways to synthesize and recycle nucleotides. Numerous recent, unbiased genomic, chemical and metabolomic screening approaches have validated nucleotide metabolism as a crucial cancer vulnerability, sparked renewed interest in the field, and helped motivate many clinical trials and drug development campaigns18–26.

Purine levels are carefully regulated by coordinated control over two complementary pathways, the de novo biosynthetic pathway and the salvage pathway. The salvage pathway recycles preformed purine bases and ribose sugars to form nucleotides, while the de novo pathway builds the purine ring from small building blocks in a multi-step, energy-intensive pathway. Compared to purine salvage, the de novo biosynthetic pathway is more highly regulated and has a greater effect on cell growth27,28. Regulation of de novo biosynthesis occurs at the gene and protein level through several feed-forward and feedback mechanisms27–30. Six cytosolic enzymes catalyze the ten highly conserved steps of this pathway31,32. In addition to generating nucleotide building blocks, an increasing number of intermediates from this pathway have been implicated in important signaling cascades and non-metabolic processes33–37.

Phosphoribosylformylglycinamidine synthase (gene name PFAS, also referred to as FGAM synthase, FGAMS or PurL) catalyzes the fourth step in the de novo biosynthesis of purine nucleotides. This enzyme is directly involved in regulating purine biosynthetic rate and is known to be a core structural element of the purinosome, a biomolecular condensate that provides spatiotemporal control over purine metabolism31,32,38–41. Increased human FGAMS (HsFGAMS) expression has also been shown to promote cancer growth. In liver cancer, specifically, high expression of this protein is strongly correlated with lower survival rates13,42. In addition, FGAMS has been directly implicated in RAS-dependent cancer cell colony formation and tumor growth18,43.

Purine metabolism is regulated post-translationally by several distinct mechanisms, with HsFGAMS playing a major role in a number of these. As with other metabolic pathways, several of the nucleotide products regulate early steps in the pathway through feedback inhibition44–46. Biosynthetic flux, spatiotemporal regulation of activity, and control over reactive intermediates are also regulated, in part, by the formation and localization of the purinosome32,38–40,47. Control over purine biosynthetic enzyme kinetics, at the individual protein level, also occur through allosteric mechanisms whereby ligand binding at a location distal to the active site induces conformational changes that influence activity48–50. All but one of the enzymes of the de novo purine biosynthetic pathway are multi-domain proteins that catalyze multi-step reactions4. The activity of several of these multi-domain proteins is regulated through interdomain allostery4,44,51,52. The enzyme that catalyzes the first committed step in the pathway, phosphoribosylpyrophosphate amidotransferase, couples activity at two distinct active sites through the allosteric regulation of a channel connecting the two sites53. Such interdomain channeling functions as a means to protect labile intermediates and facilitate direct handoff of reaction products54. Parallel allosteric control of the distinct binding sites and modulation of structural features of the channel can promote efficient catalytic coupling and be a means to subtly regulate enzyme activity.

Eukaryotic FGAMS is a multi-domain protein, representative of the large PurL (lgPurl) variants of this protein, as compared to the small PurL (smPurL) proteins, which are expressed as three distinct gene products (Fig. 1a)4,55. FGAMS catalyzes the conversion of formylglycinamide ribonucleotide (FGAR) to formylglycinamidine ribonucleotide (FGAM) (Fig. 1b). In the first, amidotransferase, reaction, ammonia is liberated from glutamine and directed to the synthase domain, where it is added to FGAR in an ATP-dependent reaction56. The transfer of ammonia between the two active sites is facilitated by a putative ammonia channel56. The presence of the channel is supported by computational and kinetic analyses, although it has not yet been physically observed nor is it clear how channel entry and exit are regulated57. FGAMS also harbors an N-terminal domain with an, as yet, unestablished role.

In this work, we describe three Cryo-EM structures of HsFGAMS, from 3.2 to 3.3 Å resolution, that capture distinct functional states and important pathway intermediates. These structures of FGAMS reveal the location and architecture of the ammonia channel and capture the proposed iminophosphate intermediate. These data also implicate the N-terminal domain as a key element involved in allosteric control of FGAMS activity. The structures and supporting kinetic analyses reveal a putative mechanism that couples the chemistry of the active sites through substrate-induced conformational changes, controlling formation of the ammonia channel as well as substrate entry and exit.

---

## Results

Expression and initial characterization of HsFGAMS
Full details about the cloning, expression, and purification of HsFGAMS are included in the supplementary information. Briefly, HsFGAMS was expressed as a C-terminally FLAG-tagged protein from HEK 293T cells and purified using immobilized affinity chromatography (Fig. 1c). Unlike the homologs from E. coli and S. typhimurium, which show a high level of basal glutaminase activity55,58–60, HsFGAMS does not exhibit observable glutaminase activity in the absence of the co-substrate FGAR (Fig. 1d). With FGAR present, the enzyme turns over glutamine with a KM of 189 ± 20 μM and kcat of 1.0 ± 0.04 s−1. Although the synthase activity of FGAMS is difficult to measure directly, we recently developed a mechanism-based assay that measures dephosphorylation of 6,8-difluoro-4-methylumbelliferyl phosphate as a surrogate for synthase activity42. Using this assay, we determined that an anomeric mixture of the substrate, α/β-FGAR, competitively binds to HsFGAMS with an IC50 of 148 ± 4 μM. As FGAMS is known to be selective for the β-FGAR anomer59, the KM for this substrate is expected to be approximately half this value.

Cryo-EM structure of the HsFGAMS-AMPPNP binary complex
To elucidate the molecular features underlying FGAMS function and as a basis for future drug discovery efforts, we sought to solve structures of FGAMS in functionally relevant states. Prior studies of S. typhimurium FGAMS (StPurL) include unliganded (3UGJ), glutamine-bound (1T3T), and glutamine/AMP-PNP (non-hydrolyzable ATP analogue) bound (3UMM) X-ray crystal structures60. Using Cryo-EM, we solved the structures of (1) HsFGAMS with AMP-PNP bound (referred to as the binary complex); (2) HsFGAMS in complex with the iminophosphate reaction intermediate and adenosine diphosphate (ADP) (referred to as the ternary complex); and 3) HsFGAMS with glutamyl thioester, AMP-PNP and FGAR bound (referred to as the quaternary complex) (Fig. 2). The ligand combinations were chosen to map the distinct steps of the catalytic mechanism, stabilize transition/intermediate states and to identify the long-range allosteric regulation network essential for the enzyme to reach its catalytically active state.

The binary complex was prepared by incubating HsFGAMS with 5 mM AMP-PNP on ice for 4 hours prior to grid preparation. We obtained an initial 3.35 Å map using C1 symmetry (Supplementary Figs. 1–3), with further 3D classification followed by non-uniform refinement yielding an improved 3.31 Å map. The final model was built using the predicted HsFGAMS structure from AlphaFold61 as a starting model. Full data collection parameters and refinement statistics are provided in Supplementary Table 1. Analysis of the binary complex structure confirms that HsFGAMS is a single polypeptide organized into three domains (Fig. 2a, b), similar to the homologous prokaryotic lgPurL structures (Supplementary Fig. 4)56. In addition to the glutaminase domain (GD, residues 1005–1335, Fig. 2 and Supplementary Fig. 5a) and synthase domain (SD, residues 173–1004, Fig. 2 and Supplementary Fig. 5b), is an N-terminal domain (NTD, Fig. 2 and Supplementary Fig. 5c) comprising residues 1–164. The SD has the expected pseudo 2-fold symmetry characteristic of this domain, consistent with a gene duplication event during the evolutionary history of this protein56. The synthase active site is found in one half of the SD, situated in a cleft formed by three subdomains (Supplementary Figs. 5b). In the other half of the SD, occupying a symmetry-related nucleotide-binding site, is an auxiliary ADP molecule (Supplementary Fig. 5b). The map shows clear density for the ADP and three associated Mg2+ ions (Fig. 3a and Supplementary Fig. 3). As there is no evidence linking this nucleotide to an enzymatic or regulatory function, the ADP is believed to play only a structural role or be a vestigial remnant of the putative duplication event that led to the formation of the SD62. The clear density distinguishing this molecule as an ADP in the binary complex, the enclosed nature of the binding site, and the fact that ADP was not present in any solutions used during purification or structural work, suggests that this molecule is incorporated during protein folding and cannot be competitively displaced by similar nucleotides, such as AMP-PNP (Fig. 3a and Supplementary Fig. 5b). The identity of the bound nucleotide was confirmed as ADP in HsFGAMS by analysis of denatured apoprotein by HPLC (Supplementary Fig. 5b).

In the binary complex of HsFGAMS, the ATP-binding site is occupied by AMP-PNP (Fig. 3b and Supplementary Fig. 3). The nucleotide binding pocket, which sits at the interface of two subdomains (Supplementary Fig. 5b), is composed of a hydrophobic pocket surrounding the adenine base (Fig. 3b, F235, F251, and F269) abutted by a loop (267–274) that forms hydrogen bonds with ribose hydroxyls and phosphate oxygen atoms. A comparison to the AMP-PCP bound PurL structure from T. maritima (TmPurL, PDB code 2HS4) suggests that additional interactions with, and charge stabilization of, the phosphates may be contributed by a metal cation that is not observable in our maps (Supplementary Fig. 6a). While the overall architecture of both the auxiliary ADP binding site and ATP binding site in the HsFGAMS SD is relatively well conserved with those of S. typhimurium and T. maritima PurL, there are several subtle but clear differences (Supplementary Fig. 6a, b). In the ATP binding site, interactions mediated by residues on the loop spanning 267-274 are distinct and dissimilar to those observed in the prokaryotic homologs (Supplementary Fig. 6a). In addition, a partially resolved, unstructured catalytic loop (C-loop, 461–479) is observed near the synthase site in the binary complex (Fig. 2a). For the prokaryote structure, this region was observed to become ordered only in the presence of FGAR at the synthase site55. Computational studies performed with the full length StPurL proposed that this loop plays a role in signal transmission and catalytic coupling between the distant active sites57.

The GD of HsFGAMS (Fig. 2b and Supplementary Fig. 5a) contains the conserved catalytic triad characteristic of the class I amidotransferase superfamily63. The catalytic cysteine (C1158) resides on a structural motif known as a “nucleophilic elbow”63. The GD interacts with the NTD primarily through hydrophobic contacts (W62, N103, I104, V107, and T111 of the NTD and V1122, G1128, A1131, and F1135 of the GD) while a series of hydrogen bonds span the GD-SD interface (N95, P99, and N102 of the NTD and D488, E490, G545, and D546 of the SD). Close examination of the HsFGAMS binary complex reveals a loop region (designated loop L1) from the NTD blocking the glutaminase active site (Supplementary Fig. 6c). The location of the L1 loop in the absence of substrate appears to be driven by an interaction between H14 on L1 and Y1237 of the GD. The presence of this 11-residue loop, and an additional, longer, solvent exposed loop (designated loop L4), are major differences setting HsFGAMS apart from the prokaryotic homologs, which do not possess these features (Supplementary Fig. 6d). However, despite low sequence identity and the presence of the loop inserts, the NTD of HsFGAMS has an overall fold that is structurally homologous to the prokaryotic PurLs of known structure (Supplementary Fig. 6e). The position of loop L1 in HsFGAMS, and its absence in prokaryotes, is suggestive of a putative role in regulating access to the glutaminase site that is distinct to the human enzyme.

Cryo-EM structure of the HsFGAMS ternary complex with trapped iminophosphate intermediate
Production of the FGAM product by FGAMS requires two separate reactions at distinct active sites (Fig. 1b). Ammonia liberated in the GD is added to FGAR in an ATP-dependent reaction. The mechanism of the synthase reaction is proposed to proceed via an activated iminophosphate intermediate55. To evaluate the architecture and allosteric regulation of the HsFGAMS SD, we prepared samples and collected Cryo-EM data for the protein with FGAR and ATP, but lacking the co-substrate glutamine. Details about sample preparation and processing are provided in the supplementary information and methods. After processing we obtained a 3.22 Å map (Fig. 2c and Supplementary Figs. 2b, 7 and 8), that was further post-processed using DeepEMhancer with individual half maps as input64, revealing additional features (Supplementary Fig. 9). The resulting map showed clearly resolved coulombic potential for a trapped iminophosphate intermediate together with an ADP molecule (Figs. 2c, d, and 3c), and a well ordered C-loop (Fig. 3d and Supplementary Fig. 8). Other alternative ligand binding modes, including ATP and FGAR or FGAR, ADP and phosphate, were not consistent with the observed density (Supplementary Figs. 10a, b). A comparison of the HsFGAMS ternary complex synthase site to that of TmPurL in complex with FGAR and AMP-PCP (PDB code 2HS4) reveals a similar binding position and orientation of the ligands and C-loop (Supplementary Fig. 10c). The ordered C-loop adopts a closed conformation in this ternary complex, shielding the synthase site and the reactive iminophosphate intermediate (Fig. 3e). This intermediate and the ADP molecule were observed to be present perpendicular to each other in the synthase site (Fig. 3e). The density also revealed the likely presence of an alternate conformer of ADP in the active pocket (Fig. 3c, e). Q485 on the C-loop makes key H-bonding interactions with the H311 and the formylglycinamide of the trapped intermediate (Fig. 3e). This interaction forms a putative anchor point that could drive the C-loop into a closed conformation. Prior computational studies using StPurL also implicated these two residues in a putative gating mechanism that controls transient channel formation65.

The SD of FGAMS belongs to the PurM superfamily of proteins, which includes selenophosphate synthase (SelD), iron-nickel hydrogenase maturation protein (HypE), and thiamine phosphate kinase (ThiL), among others66. These proteins are related by their signature DX4GAXPATP binding motif and the putative formation of an iminophosphate intermediate during catalysis. The trapped iminophosphate in the structure of the HsFGAMS ternary complex provides structural confirmation of this reaction intermediate. For FGAMS specifically, two alternate enzyme mechanisms have been proposed (Supplementary Fig. 11)67. These involve either a tetrahedral intermediate (Supplementary Fig. 11; path a) or the iminophosphate intermediate (Supplementary Fig. 11; path b) as observed in the HsFGAMS ternary complex structure. Our data, collected in the absence of an ammonia source, are consistent with phosphorylation of the δ-carbonyl of FGAR to form an iminophosphate intermediate.

Cryo-EM structure of the HsFGAMS quaternary complex with Glutamine, AMP-PNP, and FGAR
To further evaluate substrate binding, mechanism, and cooperative regulation of the distinct active sites, we incubated the protein with L-glutamine, AMP-PNP, and α/β-FGAR prior to grid preparation and data collection. From a total of 184,653 particles, we obtained a map at 3.19 Å using C1 symmetry (Fig. 2e and Supplementary Figs. 2c, 12 and 13). Further post-processing was performed using DeepEMHancer64, leading to improvements in the map, particularly in a hydrophobic linker, 3-helix bundle near the synthase site and the partially disordered C-loop (Figs. 2f, 4a and Supplementary Fig. 14). In the glutaminase active site the map was similarly well resolved to enable modeling of the substrate, which was trapped as a glutamyl thioester intermediate (Fig. 4b and Supplementary Fig. 13). In the synthase active site, there was clearly discernible coulomb potential to build the AMP-PNP and FGAR ligands (Fig. 4c, and Supplementary Fig. 13), as well as the majority of the C-loop structure (Fig. 4a–c). Similar to what was observed for the ternary complex, the AMP-PNP ligand could be built into two alternate conformations (Supplementary Fig. 13). The FGAR molecule sits perpendicular to the nucleotide, and is held in place primarily through H-bonding interactions from both the synthase binding site residues and the C-loop (Fig. 4c). When compared to the structure of the T. maritima PurL (PDB code 2HS4), the C-loop of HsFGAMS is in a more open conformation (Fig. 4d), potentially due to substrate binding at the distant GD. This configuration of the C-loop repositions Q485 away from H311 (Fig. 4c), disrupting the H-bond interaction between these two residues. This is consistent with a putative role for Q485 in regulation of intraprotein signal transmission, as proposed in previous studies65. The glutamyl thioester intermediate observed in the glutaminase active site is engaged in the primarily hydrophobic binding pocket that is highly conserved across species (Fig. 4d). Clear density was also observed at H-bonding distance from the OE2 atom of the thioester, modeled here as a water molecule (Fig. 4b, W). This marks the putative location of the initial site of the ammonia molecule immediately after liberation from glutamine.

Formation of the iminophosphate intermediate signals the GD via structural rearrangements in the NTD
The function of the NTD in FGAMS has long been unresolved. Comparison of the structures of the different states of HsFGAMS reveals distinct differences, particular between the binary (AMP-PNP bound) and ternary (iminophosphate and ADP) complexes (Fig. 5). Upon binding of the synthase substrates and formation of the iminophosphate intermediate, the NTD shifts substantially, rotating approximately 10° with respect to the GD (Fig. 5a). Accompanying this domain motion is a similar shift in a 3-helix bundle of the SD that abuts the C-loop (Fig. 5a). Conversely, other than a slight disordering of the C-loop, the overall structure of HsFGAMS in the quaternary complex was very similar to that of the binary complex (Fig. 5b).

Further analysis of these structural differences reveals several functionally relevant implications. In the ternary complex, one edge of the 3-helix bundle moves into proximity with the C-loop, forming new H-bonding interactions, specifically between G462, A465, and S468 of the C-loop and Q224 and E228 of the 3-helix bundle (Supplementary Fig. 15). The ordering and repositioning of the C-loop in the ternary complex result in a well-structured pocket surrounding the iminophosphate (Fig. 3e), presumably to protect the reactive intermediate. In addition, residues of the C-loop, which spans the region between the NTD and the 3-helix bundle, form a cation-π stacking interaction with conserved residues of the NTD (Supplementary Fig. 16). Based on the structures and supported by previous analysis of mutants57, this network plays a crucial role in intraprotein signaling between the NTD and C-loop.

This newly created NTD:C-loop interface is accompanied by conformational changes in the putative oxyanion loop, a recurring and short-lived feature common to nearly all glutaminases that stabilizes the oxyanion transition state (Fig. 6a and Supplementary Figs. 17a–d)68. Upon formation of the ternary complex, the interactions between the oxyanion loop and nearby Ω-loop, which harbors the signaling residue N107457,65, are disrupted. This results in an approximately 90° flip of the oxyanion loop and creation of the putative oxyanion hole (Fig. 6b–d). Based on the expected position of the oxyanion, movement of a section of the oxyanion loop would be necessary to accommodate the tetrahedral transition state. Our structures indicate that stabilizing interactions would be contributed through hydrogen bonding interactions with the amide nitrogen atoms of N1159 and one of the loop residues. Formation of the oxyanion hole in this manner is a proposed mechanism for substrate-dependent allosteric regulation in other glutamine amidotransferases and related enzymes, such as imidazole glycerol phosphate synthase69,70. The HsFGAMS structures suggest a critical role for the G1115-N1074 interaction in stabilizing the closed conformation of the oxyanion loop (Fig. 6b). This is consistent with previous mutational studies performed with the analogous residues in StPurL65. Upon glutamyl thioester intermediate formation, as observed in the quaternary structure of HsFGAMS, the oxyanion loop reverts back to the resting state, orienting residues G1115, G1116, and F1117 to help position and stabilize the intermediate (Fig. 6e, f).

In addition to the allosteric control through transient oxyanion stabilization, we also observed that entry to the glutaminase active site is regulated by two gates. Gate 1 is composed of H14 on the L1 loop of the NTD and Y1237 of the GD, while Y1202 and F1117 of the GD comprise gate 2 (Fig. 6a). The changes in the NTD of the ternary complex result in disorder in loop L1 (Fig. 6c), providing the needed flexibility for gating motions of H14. Similarly, these changes also impact the positioning of Y1237, yielding an open state of one of the gates (Fig. 6c, gate 1). At the same time, the loop flipping that controls transient oxyanion hole formation moves F1117 and Y1202. The latter, in particular, swings approximately 90° away from Y1202, opening this second gate (Fig. 6c, gate 2). Both of these gates return to the closed state in the quaternary complex of HsFGAMS (Fig. 6e). Note that the mechanism for gating through gate 1 is distinct to mammals, as the loop L1 region is not conserved in lower organisms (Supplementary Fig. 6c, d).

Catalytic coupling through transient ammonia channel formation
The chemistry at the synthase site of FGAMS requires delivery of the ammonia molecule produced at the distinct and distant glutaminase site. Delivery of the ammonia has been proposed to travel between the two active sites through a putative ammonia channel in the enzyme (Fig. 1b). To date, however, this channel has not been experimentally observed. In the HsFGAMS quaternary complex structure, we elucidate the architecture of this hydrophobic transient channel that passes near the auxiliary ADP binding site (Fig. 7a and Supplementary Fig. 18) using CAVER 3.0.2 PyMOL plugin71. The channel location and composition are consistent with what was predicted by MD simulations for the StPurL system (Supplementary Fig. 18)57.

Comparison of the quaternary structure to the binary and ternary complex structures reveal several key structural changes driving transient channel formation. Structure analysis showed that after glutamyl thioester intermediate formation in GD, the oxyanion loop flipped back to regain its original conformation and helped to stabilize the carbonyl group of the glutamyl moiety via hydrogen bonding interaction through its G1116 residue (Fig. 6e, f) and by closing gate 1 and gate 2 to protect the thioester intermediate in the GD (Fig. 6e). This oxyanion loop resting conformation further reverted the signal to the NTD by rotating it back by ~10o to go back in its previous conformation (Fig. 5b) via disrupting the GD and NTD interface (Fig. 6a and Supplementary Figs. 17a–d). This NTD/GD interface disruption forced the C-loop to move back in its unstructured conformation, similar to the HsPFAS-AMPPNP binary state. From moving fully ordered to fully disordered state, there is a stage when the C-loop is partially disordered. At this stage, two other gates; gate 3 (R1300-D685) at the top of the channel (Fig. 7b) and gate 4 (Q485-H311) at the bottom of the channel (Fig. 7c), are opened, which were observed to be closed in other two HsPFAS binary and ternary complexes solved here and in the previously solved StPurL and smPurL crystal structures also55,56. In brief, a salt bridge between R1300 and D685 reorganizes to form the opening of the channel at the glutaminase active site (Fig. 7b). At the synthase end of the channel, H311 is observed to block the exit in both the binary and ternary complexes, but subtle changes to Q485 disrupt the H311-Q485 interaction, opening the gate at the synthase end of the channel (Fig. 7c). The opening and closing events of these conserved gates were also highlighted in previous MD simulation studies57,65. Moreover, the mutational studies performed on gate 3 in StPurL showed a high ammonia channeling efficiency, highlighting the role of this gate in controlling ammonia release into the channel, while the mutants of gate 4 showed its dual role in gating and signal transduction to the glutaminase site65. In addition to these dual gates, additional motions were observed in the secondary structure elements on which the conserved channel lining residues reside. These residues include N394, P399, V400, S390, E398, D333, A348, T327, Y350, P423, T325, R330, T310 and M425. Additional bottleneck residues M425, Y350, and E398 obstruct the channel in the binary and ternary complexes, but change positions subtly in the quaternary complex structure to provide a clear path for the ammonia to traverse (Fig. 7a, d, and e). Mutational and crystallographic studies were previously performed on the conserved channel lining residue (V400 in HsFGAMS and V333 in StPurL) that showed a remarkable effect on the channel efficiency72. In this case, a valine to isoleucine mutation constricted the channel by ~2 Å, leading to a decrease in the synthase activity by ~20%72. Collectively, the structural changes precipitated by substrate binding and formation of the quaternary complex lead to the transient formation of the ammonia channel and provide additional gating mechanisms to regulate FGAMS activity. This type of enzyme control is not without precedent. Similar substrate-driven domain motions lead to the formation of an ammonia channel in the bacterial glucosamine-6-phosphate synthase73,74.

To confirm the role of the gating residues and transient channel formation, we generated a series of HsFGAMS mutants and characterized their relative kinetics. For all of the mutants, we determined the basal glutaminase activity, the ATP and FGAR dependent glutamate production, and overall FGAM synthesis rate (Supplementary Fig. 19a–c, respectively). While the basal rate of glutaminase activity of HsFGAMS is very low, removal of a short section of loop L1 containing gate 1 residue H14 (Δ12–15) or mutation of either of the gate 2 residues (Y1202F, F1117A), leads to a substantial increase in background glutaminase activity (Supplementary Fig. 19a). Leakage of ammonia through gate 2 is at a much higher rate, consistent with an overall motive force favoring ammonia flow from the GD to the synthase active site. As expected, the presence of ATP and FGAR does not have a large impact on the glutaminase rate for these mutants (Supplementary Fig. 19b). These mutants, however, do substantially decrease the overall rate of FGAM synthesis (Supplementary Fig. 19c). This disruption in the gating and coupling efficiency of the two domains through these subtle changes (Supplementary Fig. 19d) illustrates the importance of the tight control over substrate access and transit in FGAMS (Supplementary Figs. 19e, f). As a comparison, mutation of one of the bottleneck residues (M425K), which sits in the interior of the channel, has little impact on the glutaminase or synthase activity (Supplementary Figs. 19a–c).
